blocks.text: [III, 343] Some of the Arabs permit the eating of flies, because they are often generated from permitted things: for instance from the bean, which the Arabs say, when corrupted, is so changed into flies that nothing remains but the husk. But the Hebrews forbade flies, relying on the law found in Deut. XIV, 19. Every creeping thing that flies is unclean: it shall not be eaten. Which Jonathan paraphrases [paraphrazei] thus: וכל דיבבי וזיבורי וזיזי דטלופחי ופולי דפרשי מן אוכלא ופרחין הי כעופא מסאבין אינון לכון לא יתאכלון, all flies, and wasps (or bees) and the worms of lentils and beans which, separated from the food, fly out like a bird, shall be unclean to you; they shall not be eaten. They conclude the same from these words, Levit. XI, 20. Every creeping thing that flies and goes on four feet shall be an abomination to you. Where Jonathan has: וכל ריחשא דעופא דמהלך על ארבע זני דיבבי וזני אורעי וזני זובורי שיקצא הוא לכון ברם דיבשא דזיבורי יתאכל, And every creeping thing that flies, four-footed, the species of flies, and the species of hornets, and the species of bees, shall be an abomination to you: yet the honey of bees shall be eaten. And in the same place R. Selomo: הם הדקים הנמוכים הרחושים על הארץ כגון זבובין וצרעין ויתושין וחגבין, These are the minute little animals which creep upon the earth, such as flies, and hornets, and wasps, and locusts. If you object that flies, hornets, wasps and bees are wrongly placed by the Hebrews in the class of four-footed creeping things, since the fly kind is not τετράπους [tetrapous] but ἑξάπους [hexapous], I shall reply that the two front feet are not counted as feet, because they rather serve as hands. For they do not walk on them as on the other four; rather with them they wipe their eyes when covered with dust, take their food, and carry off whatever has to be lifted. Lucian on the fly: Ἑξάπους δὲ οὖσα, τοῖς μὲν τέσσαρσι βαδίζει μόνοις· τοῖς δὲ προσθίοις δυσὶ, καὶ ὅσα χερσὶ χρῆται. Ἴδοις ἂν οὖν αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τεττάρων βεβηκυῖαν, ἔχουσάν τι ἐν ταῖν χεροῖν μετέωρον ἐδώδιμον ἀνθρωπίνως πάνυ, καὶ καθ' ἡμᾶς [Hexapous de ousa, tois men tessarsi badizei monois; tois de prosthiois dysi, kai hosa chersi chrētai. Idois an oun autēn epi tettarōn bebēkuian, echousan ti en tain cheroin meteōron edōdimon anthrōpinōs pany, kai kath' hēmas]. Though it is six-footed, it walks on four feet only, and uses the other two in front as hands: so you may see it stepping on four feet and lifting up something edible in its hands, [col. 498] entirely in human fashion, as we do. And the Philosopher too, book 4 On the Parts, chapter 6: Τοὺς δὲ πόδας τοὺς προσθίους μείζους ἔνια τούτων ἔχει, ὅπως διὰ τὸ σκληρόφθαλμα εἶναι, ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἀκριβῶς τὴν ὄψιν ἔχει, τὰ προσπίπτοντα τοῖς προσθίον ἀποκαθαίρωσι σκέλεσιν· ὅπερ καὶ φαίνονται ποιοῦσαι αἵ τε μυῖαι, καὶ τὰ μελιττώδη τῶν ζώων· ἀεὶ γὰρ χαρακίζουσι τοῖς προσθίοις σκέλεσι [Tous de podas tous prosthious meizous enia toutōn echei, hopōs dia to sklērophthalma einai, epeidē ouk akribōs tēn opsin echei, ta prospiptonta tois prosthion apokathairōsi skelesin; hoper kai phainontai poiousai hai te myiai, kai ta melittōdē tōn zōōn; aei gar charakizousi tois prosthiois skelesi]. Some (animals) have longer front feet so that, since because of the hardness of their eyes they do not see precisely, they may wipe off with those front feet whatever [III, 344] falls into their eyes. This you may see flies doing too, and all the honey-making little animals. For they always lift up (as on stakes) anything with their front feet. So it should be rendered. For χαρακίζειν [charakizein] here is μετεωρίζειν [meteōrizein], as it is in Hesychius; not vallare [to fence with stakes] and protegere [to protect], as Gaza would have it. Pliny, book 11, chapter 48: In insects that have hard eyes the front feet are longer, so that they may wipe them with their feet from time to time, as we observe in flies. Damir: والذباب ليس له اجفان لصغر احداقه ومن شان الاجفان ان تصقل مراة الحدقه من الغبار فجعل الله له يدين يصقل بها مراة احداقه فلهذا تري الذباب ابدا يمسح بيديه عينيه [wa-l-dhubāb laysa lahu ajfān li-ṣighar aḥdāqihi wa-min shaʾn al-ajfān an taṣqul mirāt al-ḥadaqa min al-ghubār fa-jaʿala Allāh lahu yadayn yaṣqul bihā mirāt aḥdāqihi fa-li-hādhā tarī al-dhubāb abadan yamsaḥ bi-yadayhi ʿaynayhi] Flies have no eyelids because of the smallness of the pupil; but since it is the property of eyelids to wipe dust from the mirror of the pupil, God gave them hands with which to do this. So you may see them constantly wiping their eyes with these hands.

Nor was it without reason that the eating of creeping things, and among them of flies, was forbidden to the Jews: for the fly is a foul and stinking animal, born from uncleanness and gladly clinging to unclean things. And whether it comes to the tables of men or to the altars of the gods, it shamelessly plunders the feast and defiles everything by its touch. What of the fact that the tiny beast, flying into a perfumer's shop and dying by chance in an ointment box, taints all the ointment stored in it? Hence that saying of Solomon, Eccles. X, 1: One of the dead flies makes the ointment of the perfumer send forth a stench. So a little folly makes a man eminent in wisdom and honour stink. Just as Paul says that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump, 1 Cor. V, 6. For what is good is corrupted much more easily than what is bad is amended. Accordingly Haggai, chapter 2, verses 12 and 13, notes that an unclean thing is not consecrated by the touch of a holy thing; but, on the contrary, a holy thing is polluted by the touch of an unclean thing ^{(2)}.
